title: Applying exterior limewash to a rendered wall
subtitle: Brush traditional lime putty wash onto an exterior lime-rendered or masonry wall for a breathable, chalky finish
excerpt: How to make and apply exterior limewash to a traditional lime-rendered or masonry wall. Covers preparing lime putty wash, wetting the wall, applying three coats with a masonry brush, and the characteristic chalky finish.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (1880s, public domain). Traditional limewash practice documented in UK Lime Centre guidance (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin wash of lime putty or hydrated lime powder diluted with water to a consistency similar to milk or thin cream. When applied to masonry or lime render it carbonates on exposure to air and bonds to the surface. Limewash is breathable and self-repairing: small cracks close over successive coats. The characteristic chalky finish grows more attractive with recoating.

content.text: is a traditional exterior wall finish that breathes, self-repairs, and looks better with every recoat. Applied to a lime-rendered or stone wall, it protects the masonry while allowing moisture movement. Three thin coats give better coverage and durability than one thick one.

attrs.title: Lime safety
attrs.body: Lime is caustic. Wear chemical-resistant gloves and goggles when mixing and applying. If lime wash contacts skin, rinse immediately with water.

content.text: For exterior work, dilute mature lime putty with clean water to the consistency of semi-skimmed milk. The usual starting ratio is roughly 1 part lime putty to 4 to 6 parts water by volume; stir thoroughly and strain through a fine mesh to remove lumps. The wash looks thin and opaque white when wet, and dries significantly whiter. For tinted limewash, add natural earth pigments (ochre, umber, red iron oxide) to the wash and stir well; the colour fades by about 40 to 50% as the wash dries, so test on an inconspicuous patch first.

Dampen the wall with clean water immediately before applying each coat. A dry wall pulls moisture from the limewash too quickly and causes patchy adhesion. In warm or windy conditions, keep a spray bottle nearby and re-dampen any area that dries before you reach it. Do not apply limewash in direct hot sun, hard frost, or rain.

Work the limewash into the wall with a large masonry brush (the 50 mm paint brush for detail areas, a large wall brush for open areas) using circular scrubbing strokes to work the lime into the surface texture. Limewash should be worked into the wall, not painted on like emulsion. The first coat may look patchy when dry; this is normal. Allow to dry for at least two to four hours before the second coat.
Apply the second and third coats

Apply the second and third coats in the same way as the first, re-wetting the wall before each coat. Three coats are the minimum for a durable finish on a first application. On subsequent recoat visits, two coats are usually sufficient to refresh the colour and surface.

attrs.symptom: Limewash powders off the wall and does not bond
attrs.cause: Wall was too dry when coated, or the substrate is non-porous (painted concrete, modern cement render).
attrs.fix: Limewash only bonds to porous, alkaline substrates such as lime render, stone, and brick. It will not adhere to modern cement render or paint. If the wall has been painted, strip the paint before limewashing.

attrs.symptom: Uneven blotchy finish after three coats
attrs.cause: Wall dampness varied across the surface, causing the wash to absorb at different rates.
attrs.fix: Apply an extra coat on the patchy areas after dampening those sections specifically. Limewash becomes more even with successive recoating visits over the years.
